course.title: Cybersecurity Risk Management
course.description: A complete, risk-focused course for learning how organizations identify, analyze, prioritize, treat, monitor, and communicate cybersecurity risk. The curriculum connects cybersecurity scenarios to enterprise objectives and risk appetite; teaches assessment planning, likelihood and impact analysis, inherent/current/residual risk, aggregation, treatment decisions, control assurance, continuous monitoring, third-party and supply-chain risk, privacy and AI risk considerations, executive reporting, and a practical risk-register capstone. It is suitable for learners moving from foundational cybersecurity knowledge into governance, GRC, security architecture, audit, risk analysis, and security leadership work.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of computers, networks, and common cybersecurity concepts.
Familiarity with security controls, vulnerabilities, and incidents is helpful but not required.
Basic spreadsheet or text-editor skills for practical exercises.
learningOutcomes: Define cybersecurity risk scenarios using assets, threat events, vulnerabilities, likelihood, impacts, and assumptions.
Scope and plan risk assessments around business objectives, stakeholders, boundaries, and evidence.
Estimate likelihood and impact transparently and document uncertainty and confidence.
Differentiate inherent, current, and residual risk and assess whether residual risk fits organizational tolerance.
Prioritize risks using business context, dependencies, obligations, and treatment feasibility rather than raw technical scores alone.
Select and document risk treatments, exceptions, compensating controls, ownership, and reassessment criteria.
Assess control effectiveness using evidence and design/operating effectiveness concepts.
Design useful KRIs, KPIs, risk registers, and current-to-target cybersecurity profiles.
Assess third-party, supply-chain, cloud, privacy, and emerging-technology risk using proportional, context-aware methods.
Communicate cybersecurity risk clearly to technical and executive stakeholders and build an auditable risk-management workflow.
Build and validate a local cyber risk-register decision-support tool as a final assessment.

modules.title: Cybersecurity Risk Management Foundations
modules.description: Build the vocabulary, scope, and risk-thinking habits needed to manage cybersecurity risk in business context.

lessons.title: What Cybersecurity Risk Management Actually Manages
lessons.description: Distinguish cybersecurity risk management from security tooling, compliance checklists, and incident response.
learningObjectives: Explain how cyber risk affects mission, operations, assets, people, and stakeholders; distinguish risk management from technical control implementation.

notes.text: Cybersecurity risk management is the disciplined process of framing, identifying, analyzing, prioritizing, responding to, and monitoring cybersecurity risk in the context of organizational objectives. A risk program is successful when decision-makers can make defensible trade-offs, not merely when a checklist is complete.

items: Cybersecurity risk is one component of enterprise risk and should be communicated in business terms.
Risk ownership should sit with people who can make or authorize treatment decisions.
Security controls are means to reduce risk; they are not the risk itself.

notes.text: Do not equate compliance status with acceptable risk. A compliant system can still be exposed to important threats or business impacts.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes cybersecurity risk management?
options: A process for making risk-informed decisions about cybersecurity impacts and treatments
quiz.answer: A process for making risk-informed decisions about cybersecurity impacts and treatments
quiz.explanation: Risk management connects threats and weaknesses to business consequences and decisions.

summary: Risk management is decision-oriented, contextual, and continuous.
Controls should be selected because they change risk or satisfy a justified requirement.

lessons.title: Risk Appetite, Tolerance, and Capacity
lessons.description: Clarify the concepts leaders use to communicate how much uncertainty and exposure the organization can bear.
learningObjectives: Differentiate risk appetite, risk tolerance, and capacity; write a measurable tolerance statement; identify when an exception exceeds tolerance.

notes.text: Risk appetite expresses the amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or retain. Risk tolerance defines acceptable variation around objectives or risk criteria. Capacity is the practical boundary beyond which continued exposure could threaten viability or mission.

Example tolerance statement:
"No internet-facing service may retain a known actively exploited critical vulnerability beyond the emergency remediation window defined by policy."

items: Tolerance statements should be testable.
Different business processes can legitimately have different tolerances.
Risk acceptance should be authorized at the appropriate level.

practicals.title: Map Appetite to Tolerance
practicals.description: Turn a leadership appetite statement into measurable cyber-risk tolerance criteria.
steps: Write one appetite statement for a fictional organization.
Translate it into two measurable tolerances with thresholds.
Define an escalation action when a threshold is exceeded.
practicals.solution: Example answer: Appetite: protect availability of critical customer services. Tolerance: any outage of a critical service must be escalated after 30 minutes; tolerance breach triggers incident and executive notification according to the defined policy.
practicals.output: A short table with appetite, tolerance, threshold, owner, and action.

quiz.question: A risk tolerance statement should ideally be:
options: Measurable and linked to business objectives
quiz.answer: Measurable and linked to business objectives
quiz.explanation: A measurable tolerance makes risk decisions and escalations consistent.

summary: Appetite is strategic; tolerance is more operational and specific.
Good tolerance statements create clear escalation triggers.

lessons.title: Risk Terminology: Asset, Threat, Vulnerability, Event, Impact, Risk
lessons.description: Create consistent scenario language before analysis.
learningObjectives: Define the core terms; assemble a complete risk scenario; identify missing elements in weak risk statements.

notes.text:
Scenario pattern:
Asset + Threat Source/Event + Vulnerability/Condition + Likelihood + Impact = Risk Scenario

A useful cybersecurity risk scenario says what matters, what could happen, why it could happen, how likely the event is, and what consequence would follow. This is more actionable than writing "server vulnerability" as a standalone risk.
A vulnerability is not synonymous with risk. A weakness becomes materially risky only in a specific exposure and business context.

quiz.question: Which item is a consequence of a risk event rather than a threat source?
options: Loss of revenue from service outage
quiz.answer: Loss of revenue from service outage
quiz.explanation: Revenue loss is an impact; the other choices describe sources, conditions, or events.

summary: Good risk statements are scenario-based.
Separate causal chain elements so treatment can target the right point.

lessons.title: Risk Governance, Roles, and Accountability
lessons.description: Translate governance concepts into clear ownership and escalation.
learningObjectives: Assign risk owner, control owner, system owner, and decision authority; design an escalation path.

items: A risk owner has authority and accountability for how the risk is treated or accepted.
A control owner is responsible for implementing or operating a control.
The person documenting a risk does not automatically own the risk.

notes.text: Governance becomes operational when decision rights are explicit: who identifies, who evaluates, who proposes treatment, who accepts residual risk, and who monitors whether conditions changed.

quiz.question: Who should normally accept a material residual risk?
options: An authorized decision-maker with appropriate risk ownership
quiz.answer: An authorized decision-maker with appropriate risk ownership
quiz.explanation: Risk acceptance is a governance decision that requires authority.

summary: Clear ownership prevents risks from becoming orphaned findings.
Escalation criteria should be defined before a crisis.

tasks.title: Write a Defensible Cyber Risk Statement
tasks.description: Turn vague security observations into business-relevant risk scenarios.
tasks.problemStatement: Rewrite three weak findings so each includes asset, threat event, vulnerability/condition, likelihood rationale, impact, and owner.
objectives: Separate the weakness from the business impact.
tasks.hint: Ask what could happen, to what asset, through what condition, and what the business consequence would be.
tasks.solutionCode: Example: "Customer portal authentication weakness could enable unauthorized account takeover; likelihood medium due to internet exposure and missing rate controls; impact high because protected customer records could be disclosed; owner: application service owner."
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution focuses on scenario completeness and accountability rather than technical jargon alone.

modules.title: Risk Framing, Context, and Assessment Planning
modules.description: Learn how to prepare a risk assessment so the results are scoped, comparable, and useful to decision-makers.

lessons.title: Assessment Scope and System Boundaries
lessons.description: Define what is inside and outside an assessment and why boundaries influence conclusions.
learningObjectives: Set assessment scope; identify dependencies and trust boundaries; document exclusions and assumptions.

items: Identify mission/business process.
Identify assets, systems, data, identities, and dependencies.
Define organizational, technical, and time boundaries.
Record exclusions and assumptions.

notes.text: An assessment can be technically correct but decision-invalid if important dependencies are excluded without documenting the consequence.

practicals.title: Assessment Scope Worksheet
practicals.description: Create a practical scope statement for a risk assessment of a customer-facing application.
steps: State the business process and decision supported by the assessment.
List systems, data, identities, dependencies, and geographic/technical boundaries.
practicals.solution: A correct scope names the process, assets, dependencies, boundaries, exclusions, and decision deadline without pretending to assess out-of-scope components.

quiz.question: Why are explicit assessment exclusions important?
options: They clarify what conclusions do and do not cover
They guarantee the system is secure
quiz.answer: They clarify what conclusions do and do not cover
quiz.explanation: Scope limitations affect the reliability and interpretation of results.

summary: Scope is a decision boundary, not just a project-management detail.
Assumptions should be visible and testable.

lessons.title: Organizational Risk Context and Business Objectives
lessons.description: Connect cybersecurity scenarios to mission and business priorities.
learningObjectives: Identify critical business processes; map security impacts to operational objectives; capture stakeholder concerns.

notes.text: NIST risk guidance emphasizes organizational context because impact is meaningful only relative to what the organization values. Two identical technical weaknesses may have very different consequences in different business processes.

items: Identify high-value processes and services first.
Capture legal, contractual, safety, privacy, and reputational considerations where applicable.
Ask stakeholders how disruption or compromise would affect objectives.

quiz.question: What makes an impact assessment business-relevant?
options: It relates technical consequences to organizational objectives and constraints
It uses one impact scale for every context
quiz.answer: It relates technical consequences to organizational objectives and constraints
quiz.explanation: Business relevance comes from linking cyber effects to objectives and consequences.

summary: Context turns technical events into organizational risk.
Stakeholder input is essential for credible impact assumptions.

lessons.title: Threat Sources, Events, and Adversary Conditions
lessons.description: Build threat scenarios without overclaiming attacker identity or intent.
learningObjectives: Differentiate threat source, threat event, predisposing condition, and adversary behavior; document assumptions.

items: Threat source describes the origin or actor category.
Threat event describes what may happen to the target.
Predisposing conditions increase or decrease the likelihood of harm.

notes.text: Do not claim a specific actor caused an event unless evidence supports attribution. Risk assessment can use generic threat categories.

quiz.question: A missing multifactor requirement on an internet-facing account is best represented as a:
quiz.answer: Predisposing condition
quiz.explanation: The missing control changes the likelihood of a successful event.

summary: Separate threat from conditions that make events more or less likely.
Avoid unjustified attribution.

lessons.title: Risk Assessment Methods: Qualitative, Semi-Quantitative, Quantitative
lessons.description: Choose a method that fits the decision without pretending uncertain inputs are precise.
learningObjectives: Compare assessment methods; identify when a quantitative estimate is justified; document uncertainty.

notes.text: Qualitative methods use ordered categories such as low/medium/high. Semi-quantitative methods use bounded scales or formulas while retaining assumptions. Quantitative methods estimate values such as frequency and loss using data and models.
A numeric formula does not automatically make an assessment quantitative in a defensible sense. Inputs, distributions, and uncertainty need evidence and documented assumptions.

quiz.question: Which method is most likely to represent uncertainty honestly when reliable loss data are unavailable?
options: A qualitative or semi-quantitative method with explicit assumptions
A six-decimal probability generated from intuition
A fixed score that never changes
quiz.answer: A qualitative or semi-quantitative method with explicit assumptions
quiz.explanation: Using a method matched to available evidence is more defensible than false precision.

summary: Method selection should follow decision needs and evidence quality.
Uncertainty is information and should be documented.

tasks.title: Plan a Risk Assessment
tasks.description: Create a scoped assessment plan for a critical customer-facing service.
tasks.problemStatement: Produce an assessment charter covering business process, assets, boundaries, stakeholders, assumptions, assessment method, evidence sources, and decision deadline.
requirements: Use a one-page document or markdown.
tasks.hint: Start with the business decision the assessment must support, then design evidence collection around it.
tasks.solutionCode: A defensible plan names the decision, scope, evidence, analysis method, and owner/approver roles, with assumptions clearly separated from facts.
tasks.solutionExplanation: This task teaches preparation rather than premature scoring.

modules.title: Risk Identification, Analysis, and Estimation
modules.description: Move from context into repeatable identification and analysis of cybersecurity risk scenarios.

lessons.title: Asset and Data Criticality Analysis
lessons.description: Classify assets and data according to mission importance and security impact.
learningObjectives: Build a criticality model; distinguish data sensitivity from system criticality; identify dependency chains.

items: Criticality can be based on mission dependency, recovery needs, safety, legal duties, or revenue impact.
Data sensitivity and service criticality are related but not identical.
Dependencies can turn a low-criticality component into a high-impact single point of failure.

notes.text:
Example criticality fields:
process: Order Fulfillment
service: Payment API
data: Payment tokens
max_tolerable_downtime: 30 min
owner: Payment Service Owner

quiz.question: Why should dependency chains be captured?
options: Because every dependency is always critical
Because dependent systems can amplify business impact when a shared component fails
quiz.answer: Because dependent systems can amplify business impact when a shared component fails
quiz.explanation: Dependencies help reveal concentration and cascading-impact risk.

summary: Criticality should be based on business consequences.
Dependency mapping improves impact analysis.

lessons.title: Likelihood Estimation and Uncertainty
lessons.description: Estimate likelihood from observable conditions instead of intuition alone.
learningObjectives: Construct a likelihood rationale; use exposure, capability, opportunity, and control strength; record confidence.

notes.text: Likelihood estimation can consider threat capability, intent or motivation where known, opportunity/exposure, predisposing conditions, existing controls, and historical evidence. A useful assessment also records confidence in the estimate.

items: Separate inherent likelihood from likelihood after controls where the methodology requires it.
Use evidence where available and label expert judgment explicitly.
Revisit likelihood after material changes in exposure or threat activity.

quiz.question: Which addition most improves an expert-judgment likelihood estimate?
options: Documented evidence, assumptions, and confidence level
quiz.answer: Documented evidence, assumptions, and confidence level
quiz.explanation: Transparency makes judgment reviewable and updateable.

summary: Likelihood is a reasoned estimate, not a certainty.
Confidence should be visible when evidence is weak.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-30 Rev. 1 — Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments

lessons.title: Impact Analysis and Scenario Consequences
lessons.description: Model confidentiality, integrity, availability, safety, privacy, financial, and mission impacts.
learningObjectives: Write consequence chains; distinguish direct and cascading impact; map impact to business objectives.

items: State the immediate technical consequence.
Identify affected business process or service.
Describe secondary operational, legal, safety, privacy, financial, or reputational effects.
Identify duration, scale, and recovery constraints.

notes.text: Avoid double-counting the same consequence under several impact categories.

quiz.question: A database alteration causes incorrect customer balances and regulatory reporting. Which analysis approach is best?
options: Count only the number of changed rows
Trace integrity impact into business, regulatory, and operational consequences
Ignore regulatory effects because they are not technical
Treat it only as availability impact
quiz.answer: Trace integrity impact into business, regulatory, and operational consequences
quiz.explanation: Risk impact can cross technical and organizational dimensions.

summary: Impact is a consequence chain.
Secondary effects often determine business significance.

lessons.title: Inherent, Current, and Residual Risk
lessons.description: Use different risk states to explain how controls change exposure.
learningObjectives: Calculate or describe inherent risk, current risk, and residual risk; avoid assuming controls are fully effective without evidence.

notes.text: Inherent risk describes exposure before considering implemented controls in the chosen method. Current risk includes controls and conditions as they actually operate. Residual risk is what remains after planned or applied treatment.

items: Control presence is not the same as control effectiveness.
Residual risk should be compared with tolerance or acceptance criteria.
When a treatment is only planned, do not present its risk reduction as already achieved.

quiz.question: Which mistake most directly overstates risk reduction?
options: Testing a control before relying on it
Treating a planned control as if it were already operating effectively
quiz.answer: Treating a planned control as if it were already operating effectively
quiz.explanation: Planned controls do not reduce current exposure until implemented and effective.

summary: Control effectiveness must be evidenced.
Risk state should reflect actual conditions, not intentions.

lessons.title: Risk Aggregation and Common-Cause Risk
lessons.description: Understand how separate risks can combine through shared dependencies and concentration.
learningObjectives: Identify common-cause dependencies; aggregate related risks; avoid double counting.

notes.text: Risk aggregation helps leaders see enterprise exposure that is not obvious from individual records. Shared identity systems, a common cloud control plane, or a single supplier can create concentration risk across multiple processes.

items: Aggregation should preserve scenario detail while exposing common drivers.
Avoid simply adding scores from unrelated risks.
Look for common causes, dependencies, and shared controls.

quiz.question: What is a common reason to aggregate risks?
options: To identify concentration or common-cause exposure across multiple scenarios
quiz.answer: To identify concentration or common-cause exposure across multiple scenarios
quiz.explanation: Aggregation supports enterprise-level prioritization and concentration analysis.

summary: Enterprise view needs more than a list of isolated risks.
Shared causes can magnify systemic exposure.

tasks.title: Analyze a High-Value Service Risk Scenario
tasks.description: Perform a complete scenario analysis from asset criticality through residual risk.
tasks.problemStatement: Analyze an internet-facing service with a sensitive data store and produce an inherent/current/residual risk narrative.
objectives: Estimate likelihood with evidence and confidence.
Explain current controls and residual risk.
tasks.hint: Keep assumptions separate from facts and explain why the chosen likelihood/impact levels are defensible.
tasks.solutionCode: A strong solution contains a traceable scenario chain and explicitly distinguishes implemented controls from planned treatments.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The task reinforces analytical discipline without pretending to achieve false precision.

modules.title: Risk Prioritization and Treatment
modules.description: Turn analyzed risk into prioritized decisions and treatment plans tied to risk appetite and enterprise objectives.

lessons.title: Risk Prioritization in Enterprise Context
lessons.description: Prioritize risk based on enterprise objectives, tolerance, dependencies, and decision constraints.
learningObjectives: Rank a risk register; distinguish severity from priority; justify priority changes using context.

notes.text: NIST IR 8286B emphasizes prioritizing cybersecurity risk in light of enterprise objectives and adding risk response information to the cybersecurity risk register. Priority is therefore broader than an isolated technical score.

items: Priority can change when business objectives or exposure changes.
Regulatory, contractual, or safety constraints may create non-negotiable actions.
Risk aggregation can influence enterprise priority.

quiz.question: Why can two risks with similar analytical ratings have different priorities?
options: Because priority can incorporate business objectives, dependencies, obligations, and treatment feasibility
Because priority should never use context
quiz.answer: Because priority can incorporate business objectives, dependencies, obligations, and treatment feasibility
quiz.explanation: Priority is a decision layer above basic risk characterization.

summary: Separate analysis from prioritization.
Business context can legitimately change treatment order.

lessons.title: Risk Treatment Options: Mitigate, Transfer, Avoid, Accept
lessons.description: Choose and document treatment strategies rather than defaulting to "patch it".
learningObjectives: Compare treatment options; identify when risk acceptance is justified; document treatment outcomes.

items: Mitigation changes likelihood, impact, or both through controls and design changes.
Transfer shares financial or contractual consequences but rarely removes the underlying technical exposure.
Avoidance removes the risky activity or changes the architecture.
Acceptance retains the risk under authorized criteria.

quiz.question: Which treatment most directly removes an unsafe activity from the environment?
quiz.answer: Avoidance
quiz.explanation: Avoidance changes the activity or architecture so the risk source is removed.

summary: Treatment should follow the scenario and objectives.
Acceptance requires authority and documented rationale.

lessons.title: Cost, Benefit, and Risk Reduction
lessons.description: Evaluate treatment choices using expected risk reduction, implementation cost, and constraints.
learningObjectives: Compare options using risk-reduction value; include operational cost and residual risk; identify decision trade-offs.

notes.text:
Simple decision frame:
Value of treatment ≈ expected risk reduction + required obligation value - implementation/operational cost
Do not present this simple frame as a complete financial model. It is a decision aid when detailed loss modeling is unavailable.

quiz.question: Why should operational cost be included in treatment decisions?
options: Because a treatment can introduce material operational burden or new risk
quiz.answer: Because a treatment can introduce material operational burden or new risk
quiz.explanation: Treatment is a trade-off and can create secondary effects.

summary: Good decisions compare alternatives rather than assuming every control is equally valuable.
Treatment can create new dependencies or operational risk.

lessons.title: Risk Acceptance and Exceptions
lessons.description: Create defensible acceptance records and exception processes.
learningObjectives: Define exception criteria; document rationale, duration, compensating controls, owner, and review date.

items: State the risk and affected asset/process.
Explain why the normal treatment is not currently feasible.
List compensating controls.
Name the accepting authority.
Set an expiration or review date.

notes.text: An exception should not silently become permanent. Expiration and re-review are core governance controls.

practicals.title: Risk Exception Record
practicals.description: Create a time-bounded risk exception for a fictional system that cannot meet the normal treatment deadline.
steps: State the risk scenario and business reason for the exception.
Document compensating controls, accepting authority, expiry/review date, and residual-risk statement.
Define what evidence must be reviewed before renewal.
practicals.solution: A complete exception record includes a clear rationale, compensating controls, named authority, expiry/review date, and reassessment criteria.
practicals.output: A reviewable exception record rather than an informal note.

quiz.question: Which field is most important for preventing an exception from becoming invisible technical debt?
quiz.answer: Review or expiration date
quiz.explanation: Time-bounded exceptions create a governance trigger.

summary: Exceptions are controlled risk decisions.
Compensating controls should be verified just like ordinary controls.

resources.title: NIST IR 8286B — Prioritizing Cybersecurity Risk for Enterprise Risk Management
NIST SP 800-53A Rev. 5 — Assessing Security and Privacy Controls

lessons.title: Risk Treatment Plans and Roadmaps
lessons.description: Turn risk decisions into accountable, sequenced remediation programs.
learningObjectives: Write treatment milestones; assign owners; define evidence of completion; track residual risk changes.

items: Every treatment should have an owner and measurable completion evidence.
Sequence dependencies before dependent technical changes.
Recalculate or re-evaluate residual risk after implementation.

quiz.question: What should trigger a residual-risk reassessment?
options: Only the end of the fiscal year
A material treatment change, major environmental change, or new threat condition
quiz.answer: A material treatment change, major environmental change, or new threat condition
quiz.explanation: Risk is dynamic and should be reassessed when material conditions change.

summary: Treatment is a lifecycle, not a one-off ticket.
Evidence of implementation is necessary before claiming risk reduction.

tasks.title: Prioritize and Treat a Cyber Risk Register
tasks.description: Create a prioritized treatment plan for five fictional cybersecurity risks.
tasks.problemStatement: Rank five scenarios, explain the priority order, choose a treatment for each, and define owner/evidence/reassessment criteria.
objectives: Use enterprise context and risk tolerance.
Distinguish mitigation from acceptance and transfer.
Define a residual-risk check after treatment.
requirements: Use scenario facts given in the task.
tasks.hint: Prioritize against objectives and tolerance, not raw score alone.
tasks.solutionCode: The solution should provide a rationale matrix and treatment roadmap, showing which decisions require leadership acceptance versus technical execution.
tasks.solutionExplanation: This task exercises enterprise decision-making rather than vulnerability scoring alone.

modules.title: Controls, Assurance, and Continuous Monitoring
modules.description: Connect cybersecurity risk management to security controls, control assessment, and evidence-based monitoring.

lessons.title: Control Objectives and Control Families
lessons.description: Translate risk treatment into control objectives without confusing controls with outcomes.
learningObjectives: Write control objectives; group controls by purpose; map controls to risk scenarios.

notes.text: A control objective states what should be achieved. A control specifies a mechanism or practice used to achieve that objective. Control selection should trace back to risk and business requirements.

items: Preventive, detective, corrective, and compensating controls can address different points in a scenario.
Common controls can reduce multiple risks when the dependency is explicit.
A control without an owner or operating evidence is difficult to trust.

quiz.question: What is the best starting point for selecting a security control?
options: The risk scenario and the outcome the organization needs
quiz.answer: The risk scenario and the outcome the organization needs
quiz.explanation: Controls should be justified by desired risk outcomes.

summary: Controls implement risk response decisions.
Traceability improves defensibility.

lessons.title: Control Effectiveness and Assessment Evidence
lessons.description: Learn how to assess whether controls are actually designed and operating as intended.
learningObjectives: Distinguish design effectiveness from operating effectiveness; define evidence; document assessment conclusions.

items: Design effectiveness asks whether the control is capable of achieving its objective.
Operating effectiveness asks whether it is implemented and functioning as intended over time.
Evidence should be sufficient, relevant, reliable, and traceable.

notes.text: A screenshot or policy document proves existence of evidence, not necessarily effective operation.

quiz.question: Which evidence best supports operating effectiveness?
options: A policy dated five years ago
Repeated records demonstrating the control operated as intended over the assessment period
quiz.answer: Repeated records demonstrating the control operated as intended over the assessment period
quiz.explanation: Operating effectiveness requires evidence of actual operation.

summary: Assessment should test the control against its objective.
Evidence quality determines confidence.

lessons.title: Continuous Monitoring and Key Risk Indicators
lessons.description: Use KRIs and KPIs to detect changes in cyber risk and control performance.
learningObjectives: Design measurable KRIs/KPIs; set thresholds; distinguish leading and lagging indicators; trigger reassessment.

items: KPI measures performance of a process or control.
KRI signals changing risk exposure or conditions.
Thresholds should connect to action, not just dashboards.

notes.text:
Example KRI:
% of internet-facing critical assets with overdue high-risk remediation
Threshold: > 5% triggers risk review and escalation

quiz.question: What makes a KRI operationally useful?
options: It has a defined threshold and associated action
quiz.answer: It has a defined threshold and associated action
quiz.explanation: Indicators become useful when they change decisions or trigger action.

summary: Metrics should have owners and decision thresholds.
Continuous monitoring is about risk change, not constant data collection for its own sake.

lessons.title: Risk Registers, Evidence, and Auditability
lessons.description: Design a risk register that supports decisions, traceability, and audit.
learningObjectives: Define required risk-record fields; link evidence to assertions; manage record lifecycle and versioning.

items: Unique risk ID and owner.
Scenario and asset/process.
Likelihood/impact method and rationale.
Existing controls and evidence.
Response decision, due date, and residual risk.
Review history and status.

notes.text: Do not store unnecessary secrets or sensitive personal data in a risk register merely because the system supports text fields.

quiz.question: Why should evidence references be linked to risk records?
options: To let reviewers trace claims and decisions to supporting information
To remove the need for review
quiz.answer: To let reviewers trace claims and decisions to supporting information
quiz.explanation: Traceability improves confidence and auditability.

summary: Risk registers are decision records, not ticket dumps.
Keep sensitive evidence appropriately controlled.

lessons.title: NIST CSF 2.0 Profiles and Current-to-Target Gaps
lessons.description: Use Current and Target Profiles to express cybersecurity outcomes and gaps.
learningObjectives: Build a current profile; design target outcomes; prioritize gaps tied to risk.

notes.text: NIST CSF 2.0 provides organizational profiles for describing current and target cybersecurity outcomes. Comparing them helps identify and analyze gaps without requiring a single prescribed implementation technology.

items: Profiles describe outcomes rather than vendor-specific solutions.
Gap prioritization should connect to risk and organizational goals.
A target profile should be achievable and owned.

quiz.question: What is the main value of comparing Current and Target Profiles?
options: It makes gaps and desired outcomes explicit for prioritization
It removes the need for risk assessment

project.name: Cyber Risk Register and Decision Toolkit
project.description: A local command-line tool for maintaining an auditable cybersecurity risk register and generating a transparent prioritized report. It demonstrates risk scenario structure, ownership, likelihood/impact analysis, treatment tracking, validation, evidence-oriented reporting, and controlled change.
steps: Create the project directory and add the supplied files.
Validate and add a risk record from JSON.
List risks ordered by the transparent priority formula.

Review whether the report supports a treatment or acceptance decision.
Document limitations and define how an organization would govern the tool before production use.

code.README.md:
# Cyber Risk Register CLI

A defensive training project for maintaining a small, auditable cybersecurity risk register.
The tool is local-only and intentionally has no network access.

## Features
- Add risk records from JSON
- List risks by status or owner
- Compute a transparent priority score from likelihood and impact
- Produce a CSV-ready report
- Validate required fields
- Keep the risk record separate from the scoring logic

## Run
python risk_register.py init
python risk_register.py add examples/risk.json
python risk_register.py list
python risk_register.py report
code.examples/risk.json:
{
  "id": "R-001",
  "title": "Customer portal account takeover exposure",
  "asset": "Customer Portal",
  "owner": "Application Service Owner",
  "likelihood": "high",
  "impact": "high",
  "status": "open",
  "treatment": "Implement stronger authentication, rate controls, and monitoring",
  "review_date": "2026-10-01"
}

project.explanation: The project separates risk facts from derived prioritization. Each record contains an owner, scenario title, asset, likelihood, impact, status, treatment, and review date. The scoring function converts the ordered likelihood and impact categories into a transparent integer for sorting, but the course deliberately treats that score as an analytical aid rather than a substitute for enterprise judgment. Validation protects register quality; duplicate-ID checks protect record integrity; CSV reporting makes the decision set reviewable. In a production environment, the model would need stronger access control, versioning, evidence links, change approval, backup/retention, and integration with the organization’s formal risk methodology.
